entry.title: The State of Python Profiling in 2026
entry.summary: CPython now ships its own sampling profiler, free-threading is going mainstream, and coding agents have started reading profiles. In this post I look at where Python profiling stands today, compare Tachyon, py-spy, Scalene and Austin, and go through what's new in Austin 4.1.
entry.content:
Python profiling has changed more in the last two years than in the decade before. CPython 3.14 gave external tools an official way to look inside a running interpreter, and made asyncio task graphs inspectable from outside the process. CPython 3.15 ships a sampling profiler in the standard library. Free-threaded builds have gone from experiment to something people actually deploy. And a growing share of the people reading profiles aren't people at all, but coding agents.

This post looks at where things stand: what the main sampling profilers can do today, where each one fits, and what changed in the latest release of Austin.

As many of you know, I've been working on Austin for the best part of eight years now, so I have a view from the inside on how this landscape came to be, and, naturally, a soft spot for one of the tools in it. I've tried to be fair to the others: what I say about them comes from their own documentation and release notes as of October 2026. If I've got something wrong, let me know and I'll fix it.

A Quick Map of the Landscape¶

Most profilers make two basic choices, and these choices explain most of the differences between tools.

Tracing or sampling. A tracing (deterministic) profiler like cProfile records every function call and return. You get exact call counts, but the overhead changes the program's timing, sometimes a lot. A sampling profiler looks at the call stack at regular intervals and builds a statistical picture from those snapshots. You don't get call counts, but the program runs at close to normal speed. I went into the differences between the two, and how they work under the bonnet, in an earlier post.

In-process or out-of-process. An in-process profiler runs inside your program, usually by starting it for you or being imported. An out-of-process profiler is a separate program that reads the target's memory from outside. Out-of-process tools can attach to something that's already running, like a production server that started misbehaving an hour ago, without restarting it or changing its code.

All four tools in this post are sampling profilers. Tachyon, py-spy and Austin work from outside the process. Scalene works from inside.

Why These Four¶

There are many more Python profilers than I can cover here, so I've picked the ones I think are the most widely known and used, and that have a track record on accuracy and overhead. That track record isn't just my opinion. The most thorough comparison of Python profilers I know of, by the Scalene team at UMass Amherst (Berger, Stern and Altmayer Pizzorno, 2022), measured a dozen of them on the longest-running benchmarks of the pyperformance suite. Its conclusion was that sampling profilers are "both more efficient and often more accurate" than tracing ones.

The two go together. A tracing profiler runs its own code on every function call and return, inside your program, so it slows the program down, and not evenly: code that makes many small calls is slowed down far more than code that makes few, which skews the picture of where time is spent. The study found one tracing profiler reporting that a function took 80% of the run time when it actually took 25%. A sampling profiler stays out of the way of your code, so the timings it reports are much closer to how the program behaves when nobody is watching. In the study, Austin, py-spy and Scalene were among the profilers with the lowest overhead in CPU mode, adding between 0% and 2% to the run time, compared with 73% for cProfile and more than 200% for some others.

Tracing profilers still have their place: they count every call exactly, which sampling can't do. If you need to know that a function was called 1,204 times, use cProfile. If you need to know where the time goes, sample.

Tachyon is too new to have been part of that study, but as the profiler that now ships with Python, it's the one many people will reach for first, so it belongs here.

One notable absence is pyflame, Uber's profiler from 2016. It was one of the first to sample Python stacks from outside the process, and it deserves credit for showing that the approach works. But it was Linux-only, its last changes date from 2019, before Python 3.8 was released, and its repository is now archived and marked as no longer maintained. I mention a few other good tools at the end of the post.

Why Sampling Rate Matters¶

With a sampling profiler, the time attributed to a function is an estimate: the fraction of samples it appears in, multiplied by the duration of the run. Like any statistical estimate, its error shrinks as the number of samples grows, roughly in proportion to 1/√n. Sampling 10 times faster gives you about three times less noise from the same run, so short runs give stable results and short-lived functions are less likely to be missed entirely.

So the maximum rate a profiler can sustain, without disturbing the target, directly limits how accurate it can be.

That's why raw sampling speed has been a priority for Austin from the start, and it's the reason it's written in C and does nothing but sample: every microsecond saved per sample is another sample per second. Each release has pushed this further. Austin 4.0 more than doubled the maximum sampling rate of 3.x, and 4.1 pushes it higher again (more on that below), with a default of 10,000 samples per second.

Tachyon's authors clearly think the same way: the profiler is named after the hypothetical particle that travels faster than light. Its sampling core is written in C too, and while its default rate is a more conservative 1,000 samples per second, it's designed to be raised well beyond that. When a profiler that's been around since 2018 and the one that has just joined the standard library both put speed first, it's a good sign that sampling rate is finally getting the attention it deserves.

How We Got Here¶

Profiling Python from outside the process used to be close to a hack. CPython made no promises about the layout of its internal structures, so tools like Austin and py-spy had to copy large parts of the interpreter's private headers for every Python version, and work out where the interesting fields were from compiler- and platform-specific details. Every new release could break them, and often did.

Those tools showed that the approach was worth it. Being able to attach to a running process with no instrumentation and almost no overhead turned out to be winning proposition in production, and evidently it made a strong case for CPython to support out-of-process tools properly, rather than just tolerate them.

Some of that work came directly from Austin. In 2021, I made three changes to CPython, each to solve a problem I'd run into while working on Austin:

  • co_qualname (bpo-44530). Code objects only carried a function's bare name, so an external profiler couldn't tell Foo.run from Bar.run, and their samples ended up merged. Since Python 3.11, code objects also carry the qualified name, and every out-of-process profiler can show it.
  • native_thread_id (bpo-43879). To measure CPU time, a profiler needs the operating system's ID for each thread. On Linux, there was no direct way to find it from outside the process, so tools like Austin had to dig through glibc's internal thread structures to infer it. Since 3.11, the interpreter's thread state simply records it.
  • Py_Version (bpo-43931). An exported symbol that lets external tools reliably tell which Python version a process is running. py-spy now uses it too.

Tachyon reads both co_qualname and native_thread_id today. In 2023 I moved the fields that out-of-process tools rely on to the top of the interpreter's structures (gh-105271). That change was one of the references Pablo Galindo cited when he proposed the debug offsets table (gh-106597): a structure at the start of the runtime state that tells external tools where to find the data they need, without copying any headers. I later added more fields to it (gh-121311). The debug offsets table is the foundation that PEP 768's remote debugging interface is built on, and that Tachyon uses to read the interpreter's state.

So the profiler that now ships with CPython is, in a sense, the result of years of external tools proving that out-of-process sampling works. CPython made it a supported use case, and the core developers have now built a sampling profiler into the interpreter itself. I find that very satisfying, and it's good news for every external tool too, Austin included.

Tachyon: A Profiler in the Standard Library¶

The biggest news of the year is that CPython 3.15 includes a sampling profiler, profiling.sampling, also known as Tachyon (it was proposed alongside reorganising cProfile into profiling.tracing, in PEP 799). It builds on the remote debugging support added in 3.14 by PEP 768.

python -m profiling.sampling run --flamegraph script.py
python -m profiling.sampling attach 12345
python -m profiling.sampling run --live script.py

Tachyon covers a lot of ground for a first release:

  • run a script, attach to a running process, or dump its current stacks.
  • Wall time, CPU time, GIL-holding and exception sampling modes.
  • An --async-aware mode that rebuilds stacks per asyncio task.
  • A live, top-style terminal view.
  • Many output formats: pstats, collapsed stacks, interactive HTML flame graphs and line-level heatmaps, differential flame graphs, the Firefox Profiler's Gecko format, JSONL, and a compact binary format.
  • Subprocess profiling, and a default sampling rate of 1 kHz that can be raised.

The obvious advantage is that it's already there: nothing to install, and it's maintained alongside the interpreter, so it stays in step with internal changes.

The main limit is version coverage. Tachyon only profiles Python 3.15 and later, and the profiler and the target must run the same minor version (and the same build type: free-threaded or standard). If your services run on 3.12, Tachyon doesn't help you yet. Its --native option adds placeholder <native> frames to show where Python calls into native code, but doesn't unwind the native stack itself.

A Familiar Design¶

If you've used Austin, much of Tachyon will feel familiar. The basic approach of reading the interpreter's memory from outside the process is shared with py-spy, and goes back to pyflame in 2016. But beyond that, many of the features Tachyon has added since its first commit in August 2025 are ones Austin has had for years:

Feature In Austin since In Tachyon since
Separate wall time and CPU time modes 0.2 (2018) September 2025
Profiling child processes 1.0 (2019) December 2025
Marking samples taken during garbage collection 3.1 (2021) November 2025
Writing raw samples to a compact binary format, analysed later 3.4 (2022) December 2025
Column-level source locations in that format 3.5 (2023) December 2025
Sampling all sub-interpreters 3.6 (2023) September 2025

Some of these exist in py-spy too, and it goes the other way as well: Tachyon's asyncio support landed before Austin's. That's how open source should work, with good ideas spreading between projects. What's missing is the credit. PEP 799 doesn't mention Austin, py-spy or any of the external profilers whose approach Tachyon adopts. I think that's a missed opportunity to recognise the years of community work that came before the standard library caught up, and that made it possible. ~Update 2026-11-06 Since this post was first published, the core developers have added an acknowledgement to Tachyon's documentation and to What's New in Python 3.15 (gh-161445), recognising Austin, py-spy, Pyflame and rbspy, and thanking "their authors and the wider profiling community for their work and ideas". Thank you! It's a small paragraph, but it means a lot to everyone who spent years building these tools before the standard library caught up. Revision log

py-spy: The Established Choice¶

py-spy, written in Rust, made out-of-process sampling mainstream for Python, and it's what many people mean when they say "Python sampling profiler".

py-spy record -o profile.svg --pid 12345
py-spy top --pid 12345
py-spy dump --pid 12345

Its record, top and dump commands are a model of a simple interface. It writes SVG flame graphs, Speedscope and Chrome trace files, can follow subprocesses, filter to threads holding the GIL, and include or exclude idle threads. With --native it also unwinds native C, C++ and Rust frames on Linux (x86_64 and, since recently, aarch64) and Windows.

py-spy 0.4.2, released in April 2026, added Python 3.14 support. At the time of writing, free-threaded builds aren't supported yet (there's an open issue tracking it), and there's no task-aware asyncio mode: coroutines appear as ordinary frames on whichever thread runs the event loop.

Scalene: The In-Process All-Rounder¶

Scalene takes a different approach. It runs your program for you and profiles from the inside, which lets it measure things external tools can't easily see.

scalene run script.py

Its strengths are breadth and line-level detail:

  • CPU time split into Python, native and system time, per line and per function.
  • Memory profiling through its own allocator, including per-line allocation, likely leaks, and copy volume (for example, data accidentally copied between NumPy and Python objects).
  • GPU time on NVIDIA GPUs, and on Apple GPUs when using PyTorch's MPS backend.
  • Wall-clock await time per line for async code, along with how many coroutines were waiting there at once.
  • Combined Python and native stacks, shown as flame charts and a timeline.
  • AI-generated optimisation suggestions from the web UI, using a provider of your choice (OpenAI, Bedrock, Azure or a local model through Ollama).

Two of these numbers come with caveats. Scalene doesn't observe native code directly: it uses a timer signal, and treats any delay in handling it as time spent in native code, during which Python can't handle signals. But CPython only handles signals on the main thread, so in a program with several busy threads the delay can simply come from waiting for its turn on the GIL. In 2022, Pablo Galindo showed a multi-threaded, pure-Python program that Scalene reported as spending most of its time in native code (scalene#428). Scalene's author replied that worker threads are profiled in a different way, but the issue is still open, and the current code still estimates the main thread's native time from the signal delay. So treat the Python/native split with some care in multi-threaded programs.

For GPU time on NVIDIA, Scalene needs the GPU's per-process accounting mode, which has to be enabled once with root privileges. Without it, Scalene falls back to the utilisation of the whole GPU, including other processes, and shows a warning saying so.

Scalene 2.4 (October 2026) supports free-threaded Python 3.13 and 3.14. By its own figures, the overhead is typically 10–20%. That's fine during development, but the trade-off of being in-process is that you can't attach Scalene to something already running. You have to start the program under it.

Austin: Sampling from the Outside, at Speed¶

Austin is the tool I maintain. It's a frame stack sampler written in pure C, with no dependencies beyond the C standard library and the operating system. It reads the interpreter's memory from outside the process, writes every sample to a compact binary format called MOJO, and leaves the analysis to other tools. Because it doesn't aggregate anything while it samples, it can sample very fast.

austin -o profile.mojo python script.py
sudo austin -p 12345 -o profile.mojo
austin -w 12345   # print the current stacks of every thread

Austin 4.1 supports CPython 3.10 through 3.15, including free-threaded builds, on Linux, macOS and Windows. On Linux it also runs on less common architectures like i686, armv7 and ppc64le. Each release drops the oldest Python versions, but older releases of Austin are still available if you need to profile something older: Austin 4.0 supports 3.9 through 3.14, 3.7 supports 3.8 through 3.13, and 3.5 goes all the way back to Python 2.3.

Austin 4.1 adds four things worth covering in some detail.

1. Higher Sampling Rates¶

Austin 4.0 already more than doubled the maximum sampling rate of the previous release, by cutting down how much memory Austin reads from the target and how much work it does to write each sample. 4.1 goes further: Austin now detects when a thread's stack hasn't changed since the previous sample. When that happens, it skips walking the stack again and writes a short "same as before" marker instead of the whole stack, which also makes the output files smaller. It also buffers its output instead of writing each sample separately.

Every performance change to Austin is benchmarked in CI against the code it replaces, and the results are posted on the pull request. Here are the two that made the biggest difference, measured on Linux (x86_64) with Python 3.13, at the smallest sampling interval (1 µs), where Austin samples as fast as it can:

Change Maximum sampling rate (wall time) Time per sample
4.0 performance work, compared with Austin 3.7 (#295) 54,000 → 111,000 samples/s (×2.1) 32.4 → 12.4 µs
4.1 repeated stack detection (#402) 121,000 → 166,000 samples/s (+37%) 15.0 → 10.4 µs

In CPU time mode, where Austin also has to check whether each thread is on the CPU, the same changes took the maximum rate from 20,000 to 32,000 samples per second (+60%) and from 34,000 to 37,000 (+9%) respectively.

Something to keep in mind is that the gain from repeated stack detection depends on how often stacks repeat between samples. That happens a lot when a program spends time in long-running loops or calls, but it varies with the workload.

As explained earlier, this matters for accuracy: at the default 100 µs interval, Austin collects up to 10,000 samples per second per thread, ten times Tachyon's default rate.

2. Native Mode¶

With -n/--native, Austin collects native call stacks and interleaves them with the Python frames they belong to:

austin -n -i 1ms -o profile.mojo python script.py

This shows, for example, what's actually happening inside NumPy, a Cython module or a Rust extension built with PyO3, not just that time was spent "somewhere in native code". In native mode Austin also samples threads that never run Python code, like worker threads started by native libraries, which are invisible to profilers that only look at Python threads.

Austin users may remember that native stacks used to need a separate tool, austinp, a variant of Austin that uses libunwind to walk native stacks. It was a separate tool for two reasons. It only worked on Linux. And it broke one of Austin's founding principles, minimal impact on the program being profiled: to walk a thread's native stack reliably, libunwind needs the thread to stand still, so austinp had to stop each thread while sampling it. I wrote about that trade-off in Spy on Python down to the Linux kernel level.

The new native mode fixes the first problem. It works on Linux (x86_64 and aarch64), macOS and Windows (x86_64), with no extra dependencies, because Austin now walks native stacks itself instead of relying on libunwind. Its design owes a lot to samply, Markus Stange's excellent native sampling profiler, which showed how fast and portable this kind of unwinding can be. On macOS, Austin captures native stacks the same way samply does. On Linux, both unwind using the compiler-generated unwind tables, though they capture stacks differently, and on Windows samply relies on the system's event tracing while Austin unwinds stacks itself. As far as I know, Austin is currently the only out-of-process Python profiler that unwinds native stacks on macOS. austinp is still available on Linux, for the architectures that native mode doesn't cover yet and for sampling kernel stacks.

There is one other way to get Python and native frames in the same profile. Since 3.12, CPython can make Python function calls visible to native profilers like perf and samply (on macOS from Python 3.15), if you enable its perf support with -X perf or PYTHONPERFSUPPORT=1. You get Python function names in a fully native profile. But it has to be enabled inside the target process, it only goes down to functions, not lines, and it slows Python down: in 2023 Mark Shannon measured an 8% slowdown on a standard build, with more expected in builds that keep frame pointers. So it's a good option for a quick look at a local program, rather than for attaching to something already running.

The second problem is a deliberate compromise. To get a consistent native stack, Austin still has to briefly suspend each thread while sampling it, so native mode has more impact on the program than Austin's normal mode, and the impact grows with the sampling rate. Use a larger interval (1 ms is a good start), and avoid it in production. That's why native mode is an option you turn on, not the default. In its normal mode, Austin still never pauses the program it's profiling, and I explained the reasoning behind that in an earlier post.

3. asyncio Profiling¶

On CPython 3.14 and later, Austin tracks the asyncio task graph: each event loop's tasks, the coroutine chain each task is executing or suspended at, and which tasks are awaiting which. Samples are attributed to the task running on the thread, and the stacks of suspended tasks are recorded together with the await relationships between them.

That's what you need to answer the question that ordinary flame graphs get wrong for async code: not "which frames were on the CPU", but "which task was slow, and was it slow because it was working or because it was waiting on something else?" And austin -w prints the live task tree of a running application, grouped under the thread whose event loop owns it.

There's a further difference that's easy to miss. Most sampling profilers only record what was running, so each sample is anonymous: they can tell you that fetch_user took 30% of the time, but not whether that was one slow task or a thousand quick ones. Tachyon's async-aware mode labels each stack with the name of its task, but still adds the samples up into a single aggregate profile. Austin records which task each sample belongs to, and follows each task from the first time it sees it to the last. That makes its asyncio support closer to a tracer in spirit, while keeping the low overhead of sampling.

The VS Code extension makes use of this. Alongside the usual flame graph, which adds up time across all tasks, its Task Trace panel shows a flame chart for each event loop: every task drawn from when it was first seen to when it was last seen, nested under the task awaiting it, with how much of that time it spent running and how much waiting. So you can see what happened over time, not just where the time went in total, which is often what you need to work out why a request was slow.

4. Making Profiling Approachable¶

Here's an uncomfortable truth: most Python code never gets profiled. Not because the tools are missing, but because profiling feels hard to get into. You have to pick a tool, run it the right way, and then make sense of a flame graph full of frames you've never heard of. Many developers try it once, feel lost, and go back to guessing. That's a shame, because as I argued in How to bust Python performance issues, a single profiling run often turns up easy wins. A big part of what I want Austin to do is lower that barrier, and 4.1 approaches it from two directions.

Let an agent do the work. Coding agents can now profile code with Austin and reason about the results themselves. You ask "why is this endpoint slow?", and the agent runs Austin, finds the hot path, proposes a fix, and profiles again to check that the fix worked. There are two ways to set this up:

  • The VS Code extension includes an MCP server that exposes the loaded profile to agents. Its data tools let the agent ask for the hottest functions, call stacks, asyncio task traces, GC activity and metadata. It works with GitHub Copilot's agent mode with no setup, and with Claude Code, Cursor or any other MCP client after running a single command.
  • The austin-python package has a query API that answers the same questions in plain Python, and a command-line front-end for it, austin-query, that prints the results as text tables or JSON. Any agent that can run shell commands can use it, in a terminal, a script or CI. Pointing the agent at austin-query --help is usually all the setup it needs.

The command line is a good place to start, but agents get more out of the Python API behind it. Each query returns typed objects rather than text, so the agent can write a short script that hands them over to other libraries: pandas to compare two profiles, a plotting library to chart the results, or the project's own code to work out which component owns each hot function. An analysis that would take a long chain of CLI calls, each one reading the profile again, becomes a few lines of Python over a profile loaded once. The selectors and filters are the same as on the command line, e.g. q.filter(thread="main").callers("db.py:execute"), so the agent can move from one to the other without learning anything new. For example, this is all it takes to see which functions got faster, or slower, after a fix:

import pandas as pd
from austin.query import ProfileQuery

def hot(path):
    return pd.Series({
        f"{e.location.filename}:{e.location.function}": e.own_pct
        for e in ProfileQuery.from_file(path).top(50)
    })

change = hot("after.mojo").sub(hot("before.mojo"), fill_value=0)
print(change.sort_values().to_string())

A word of caution, though: a single pair of profiles is a shaky basis for a verdict. Sampling, and the system itself, add noise from one run to the next, so part of the change above could be nothing more than that. For a rigorous answer, pyrometry is a small library of mine that implements the ideas of On the Algebraic Properties of Flame Graphs. It treats flame graphs as vectors that can be added, subtracted and averaged, and it compares two sets of profiles, say five runs before a change and five after, with a statistical test (Hotelling's T²), keeping only the stacks whose difference is significant. The result is then split into the stacks that appeared, disappeared, grew or shrank. That's out of reach for a chain of CLI calls, but it's a short script for an agent with the Python API, and pointing it at pyrometry gives it a sound method to follow instead of eyeballing two flame graphs. Nor is this just theory: Austin's own CI uses the same test to validate every pull request. It profiles the same scenarios ten times with the base branch and ten times with the changes, on every supported version of Python, and checks that the new build still reports the same data as the old one.

Or let it teach you. Having an agent fix things for you is useful, but it doesn't make you any better at reading a profile. So the MCP server also has action tools that let the agent search and zoom the flame graph in the editor, while you watch. That turns the extension into a learning tool: instead of "fix this", you can ask your agent to walk you through the analysis. It can zoom into the hot path and explain why it's hot, point out the frame where your code hands over to a library, or show you what time spent waiting looks like compared with time spent computing. You're both looking at the same flame graph, so after a few sessions you start to recognise the patterns yourself, and the next time, you might not need to ask. Busting performance issues, AI edition shows both approaches on a real project, including one of these guided tours.

Other Things in 4.1¶

The rest of the release is about meeting Python where it's going, and where it actually runs. Austin 4.1 supports Python 3.15 on day one, and free-threaded builds too. Free-threading changes a lot for a profiler: without the GIL, threads really do run at the same time, so a sampler has to keep up with all of them at once. The one thing it costs is some accuracy in memory mode, since without the GIL there's no reliable way to tell which thread caused a change in memory usage (see below).

Profiles are also easier to read. Threads now show up under the names you gave them in the threading module, so you see MainThread and worker-3 rather than a list of opaque thread IDs, which makes a big difference in a busy multi-threaded application.

Finally, a lot of Python runs in containers, and profiling it from the host used to be awkward. Austin 4.1 handles containerised processes better, and it now records the target's working directory, virtual environment and PYTHONPATH alongside the samples. That's the information a tool needs to map the file paths in a profile back to the source files on your machine, even when the code ran somewhere else.

Where Austin Falls Short¶

Whilst Austin has a memory mode, users must be aware that it isn't an allocation profiler. Its memory mode measures changes in resident memory (RSS) between samples: how much physical memory the process is actually using, not how much it has asked for. These can be very different numbers. If you allocate a 512 MB array but only write to half of it, the operating system only provides physical memory for the half you've used, so RSS grows by about 256 MB.

That's exactly the test the Scalene study used to compare memory profilers: allocate 512 MB, touch between 0% and 100% of it, and check that the profiler reports 512 MB. Austin mostly reported less, and the study counted that as inaccurate. But reporting only the memory that was touched is the correct answer for what Austin measures. The study was asking an allocation question, and Austin answers a residency question. Both are useful: RSS tells you what your process really costs the machine, which is what matters when you're about to run out of memory. But if you want to know which line allocated what, or hunt for leaks, you want an allocation profiler like Scalene or memray. Austin also has no line-level GUI of its own. It relies on the VS Code extension, the TUI, Speedscope or pprof for visualisation, so out of the box it asks a bit more of you than Scalene or py-spy do. And attaching to a process needs elevated privileges on Linux and macOS, as it does for any out-of-process profiler.

Which One Should You Use?¶

There isn't one best profiler. Here's how I'd choose:

  • You're on Python 3.15 and want something quick: start with Tachyon. It's already installed, and it's good.
  • You need to know about memory or GPU time, line by line: use Scalene, as long as you can start the program under it.
  • You need to profile older Python versions, or attach to production: py-spy and Austin both do this well. Austin covers 3.15 and free-threaded builds today, and samples faster.
  • You're profiling asyncio code: on 3.14+, Austin gives you task-level profiles that account for waiting time, Tachyon gives you task-aware stacks on 3.15, and Scalene tells you which await lines are slow.
  • You're working on native extensions, especially on macOS: use Austin's native mode.
  • You want your coding agent to do the profiling, or to teach you how: use Austin's MCP server or austin-query.

Other tools worth knowing about: pyinstrument for a friendly in-process call tree, memray for serious memory work, and cProfile (now profiling.tracing) when you need exact call counts.

What's Next¶

Python profiling has never been in better shape. Having a sampling profiler in the standard library raises the baseline for everyone, and the remote debugging work in 3.14 and 3.15 makes all external tools more reliable. I expect the next round of progress to come from two directions: better support for concurrency (free-threading and asyncio together), and making profiling accessible to everyone, whether that means an agent doing the work or an agent teaching you to do it yourself. The best profiler is the one people actually use.

Austin 4.1 is available on PyPI, Homebrew, Snap, Chocolatey, Scoop, conda-forge and as standalone binaries from GitHub releases. The documentation covers everything above in more detail. If you try it, I'd love to hear how it goes.

entry.title: Busting performance issues, AI edition
entry.summary: Coding agents are fast becoming the main generators of new source code, but they are also being used for code review, finding and fixing bugs. How can they be used to the best extent to discover and fix performance issues?
entry.content:
In a previous post we looked at how to find and resolve performance issues lurking in any codebase by simply running some of its code through a profiler. The simplest thing we can do, especially when we come to a new codebase that is totally unknown to us is to run its test suite (or a subset of it) and see what code paths are being exercised. When we look at them through a profiler, the typical approach is to start investigating its plateaux, that is functions at the top (or bottom, depending on the orientation of the flame graph!) that have the largest own time. This is generally where the largest opportunity of improvements are. Of course, there could be cases where a function is simply repeating unnecessary work, and this won't show up through a mere visual plateau scan.

Enter AI¶

Can we automate this process, and perhaps put it on steroids, with the prowess of the most powerful, state-of-the-art coding agents?

Modern coding agents have reached a level of sophistication where they can effectively understand and modify codebases with good practical results. Benchmarks such as SWE-bench (which tests multi-file bug fixes in real GitHub repositories) and LiveCodeBench (which uses fresh competitive programming problems to avoid data contamination) show that frontier models now achieve high pass rates. However, there still is quite the margin for improvement: studies on real-world class-level code generation show a significant gap between synthetic benchmark performance (84-89%) and actual project performance (25-34%) (arxiv-2510.26130), highlighting both the progress made and the room for improvement in practical coding scenarios.

In this post we will explore how well a coding agent can come up with performance improvements when it is provided with focused profiling data. The focus, however, is on the method and the tooling involved, rather than benchmarking a set of models to determine which one is better at finding performance issues.

bytecode: Our Case Study¶

To make the exposition concrete we will focus on an actual project: we will try to improve the performance of the bytecode library.

bytecode is a Python library for generating and modifying Python bytecode. It provides an abstraction over Python's low-level bytecode instructions, allowing you to programmatically create bytecode objects, convert them to actual code objects, and even inspect and modify existing code's bytecode. It is useful for metaprogramming, dynamic code generation, and bytecode analysis.

These are the tools that we will use for our little experiment, all free:

  • Austin, for Python profiling, easily installed with "pip install austin-dist"
  • The Austin VS Code extension, easily installed from the VS Code marketplaces. The latest version comes with an MCP server that can feed profiling data and flame graph navigation commands to a coding agent.
  • Opencode with the MiniMax M2.5 free model as our coding agent setup.
  • The Opencode VS Code extension to never leave VS Code throughout our experiment

A Bit of Setup Required¶

After having cloned the bytecode repository that we will be working on, and opened it in VS Code, there is a minimum of setup required. We need to allow the coding agent to discover the Austin MCP. If you're using GitHub Copilot instead of Opencode, there is no extra setup required for this, since the Austin MCP server integrates natively with that. Otherwise we need to allow other coding agents to discover the server. This is as simple as running the Austin: Generate .mcp.json command: press Ctrl+Shift+P, type austinmcp and press Enter. That's it. Well, not quite, because we decided to use Opencode for our experiment, and as at the moment of writing, it still does not support a .mcp.json file. So instead we open an Opencode session with Ctrl+Escape and politely ask the agent to convert the .mcp.json configuration to something that opencode understands

The Austin MCP server uses an ephemeral port to run, so every time you re-open VS Code there will be a new port assigned to it. If a .mcp.json was previously created, the Austin extension will update the port automatically so that you don't have to regenerate it every time. However, Opencode won't do this unless you instruct it to.

After Opencode configured itself, you might have to start a new session for it to pick up the connection to the server.

Finally, let's create a virtual environment where we can install the library in editable mode so that we can quickly test our changes. Pick your favourite version of Python (one that the library supports of course, e.g. 3.13) and run

cd /path/to/bytecode
python3.13 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e .

After this we're all set to start experimenting!

Establishing the Baseline¶

As a first step, we should probably try to establish a baseline. This will give us a sense of where we're starting from in terms of the performance to make sure that we have a clear signal that the changes that the coding agent is coming up with are actually improving things. For our case at hand, we can use a simple round-trip benchmark run: we take a reference code object, decompile and recompile it in a loop for about 1 second. We can then measure how many times we were able to do this, which will be our throughput metric. Our baseline was 203 iterations per second. Meanwhile, we can also profile the benchmark to see what codepaths are being exercised and what they look like in terms of wall time distributions.

Here we won't bother too much with wall vs. CPU time because we expect the work to be essentially single-threaded CPU-bound anyway.

So this is the simple script that we will be using to drive the analysis

# perf.py

import bytecode
from time import perf_counter as time

code = bytecode.ConcreteBytecode.to_code.__code__

end = time() + 1.0
c = 0
while time() < end:
    c += 1
    bytecode.Bytecode.from_code(code).to_code()
print(c)

The output to screen is the plain throughput, so this will give us an immediate feedback when we run it. So let's run it and take note of the output, and to complete our baseline let's grab a profile as well

austin -o perf.mojo python perf.py

Communicating Our Intent to the Agent¶

Now that we have our baseline, let's state our intent with the agent and ask it to analyse the profiling data we have just collected.

Because the agent has access to the Austin MCP tools, it can easily figure out that it needs to use the load tool to open the profile. It can then use the other tools to pull meaningful profiling data, such as the top functions in terms of own time (the plateau analysis) and the call stacks. This allows the agent to focus on areas of the code base that the profile has highlighted as requiring attention, instead of getting lost in the entirety of the source code. Immediately the agent comes back to us with some ideas.

On a Mission¶

Galvanised by the early success, the agent gets very eager to implement more and more improvements, quickly spiraling into an iteration loop where it autonomously runs and profiles the benchmark script.

We ask the agent to include test runs in the loop to make sure that its changes are not breaking anything and it complies immediately

Now we're not here to advocate for this or that model (I have obtained much better results with more powerful models), but we've already achieved a +17% improvement (203 → 237 iterations per second) in just a few minutes of running this experiment using completely free tools, so this is already a pretty good win. We can maybe push things a bit further with some human input. For example, looking at the Top View from the Austin side panel, we notice that dis shows up at the top in terms of own time and we might wonder if we can bypass its overhead for something more direct for our needs.

A Guided Tour of Profiles¶

Reading a profile is generally not an easy task, especially when you jump into a code base that you are not familiar with, and the profile looks "hairy": many spiky peaks and small plateaux that don't really give you an immediate lead for a performance investigation. Because coding agents can understand a code base very quickly and reason about code paths, allowing them to utilise profiling data to drive their analysis means that we can put performance analysis on overdrive with the right set of tools. But while allowing an agent to figure out performance issues is nice and cool, especially because of the satisfying wins, one might still want to be kept in the loop and know what the agent is thinking. The tools exposed by the Austin MCP server allow us to ask the agent to show us around the profile in a sort of guided tour. So we could, for instance, ask it to show us the relevant part in a profile where it is considering making performance optimisations, and why. This might help the user develop a better intuition of how to use profiles, essentially using the coding agent as a tutor that can instruct how to read a profile.

A Bonus: Learning to Read Profiles¶

So beyond just fixing issues, there's a hidden gem in this workflow: you can use the agent as a learning tool. Instead of just handing off the problem, try asking it to explain what it's looking at:

  • "What does this plateau tell us?"
  • "Why is this function taking so long compared to others?"
  • "What's the call path to this hot function?"
  • "What would you look for next in this profile?"

Over time, this might help you build intuition for reading profiles yourself, if you have never dived into one before, or you have only skimmed some briefly. The agent doesn't get tired of explaining, and you get a personalised tutorial every time you run a new profile. This turns a powerful but esoteric tool like a profiler into something more accessible, an assistant that can teach you at your own pace.

Is Profiling Data Really Necessary?¶

One observation that can be made at this point is how relevant profiling data is in this process. Would the agent been able to identify the same performance issues in the code without consulting any profiling data and by just looking at the code? To try answer this question, I have repeated the experiment, starting from the same commit, and I have asked the agent to identify any optimisation opportunities just by looking at the code

Perhaps unsurprisingly, after a first scan of the code, the agent feels the need to reach out for a profiler (cProfile from the Python standard library in this case) to guide its analysis.

However, even with that data now at its disposal, it struggles quite a bit to decide what needs to be optimised. It looks as if it had identified the repeated validation issue, but it's not quite sure it is the best path to take. After 15 minutes the agent is still debating on what to do.

When asked where we are in terms of gains after some attempts at reducing some repeated operations, the agent replies that the gains are still quite marginal and that it needs to think about the code more.

Half an hour in we still haven't breached the 5% barrier, and when I ask the agent to validate its changes by running the test suite we discover a segmentation fault.

One fair conclusion we can draw from this is that indeed profiling data matters, as well as the quality of the data itself. Quite likely, the Austin MCP server was able to feed the agent with more fine-grained, detailed profiling data that allowed it to focus on the areas of the codebase that really needed attention to find those performance optimisation opportunities. With lower quality data, or with the lack of it, the agent feels a bit lost and tries to reach for that missing information by itself.

The Takeaway¶

Our experiment has highlighted that a coding agent, when equipped with good quality profiling data, can find genuine performance improvements without much hand-holding. Our baseline of 203 iterations per second jumped to 237 with about 15 minutes of agent time and no manual profiling or code inspection on our part. The agent identified an O(n²) algorithm, inlined hot paths, and eliminated unnecessary validation. Instead, when profiling data was missing or not so fine-grained, the agent struggled to find any solid and correct improvements.

So take that project you've been meaning to optimise, fire up a good profiler, and ask your favourite coding agent to take a look. You might be surprised how far a little profiling data goes.

entry.title: Running C unit tests with pytest
entry.summary: In this post I will describe my approach to C unit testing using pytest. In particular, we get to see how to gracefully handle SIGSEGVs and prevent them from stopping the test runner abruptly. Furthermore, we shall try to write tests in a Pythonic way.
entry.content:
Why?¶

That's probably what you might be asking right now. Why use a Python testing framework to test C code? Why don't just use C testing frameworks, like Google Test, or Check. I can give you an answer with all the reasons that led me to adopt pytest as the testing framework of choice for one of my C projects, Austin. The first is that I spend most time coding in Python these days and I have more familiarity with pytest than any other testing framework. Secondly, whilst Austin is a C project, it actually targets Python programs, so Python is already one of the testing dependencies that ends up being installed in CI anyway. Hence, instead of spending time learning an entire new testing framework, I could quickly write them in Python, and leverage all the features of pytest, as well as all the packages that are available for Python, should I ever need to. But these are not all the reasons for adopting pytest for running C tests. If you keep reading you will discover a few more that might convince you to use pytest for your C unit tests too!

Calling native code from Python¶

Testing C code with Python would only make sense if it were easy to call native code from the interpreter. Thankfully, the Python standard library comes with the ctypes module that allows us to do just that! So let's start looking at some C code, for instance,

# file: fact.c

long fact(long n) {
    if (n < 1)
        return 1;
    return n * fact(n - 1);
}

which we want to compile as a shared object, e.g. with

gcc -shared -o fact.so fact.c

How do we test the fact function from Python? Easy peasy!

# file: fact.py

from ctypes import CDLL

libfact = CDLL("./fact.so")

assert libfact.fact(6) == 720
assert libfact.fact(0) == 1
assert libfact.fact(-42) == 1

Assuming we are in the directory where both fact.so and fact.py reside, we can test the fact function inside fact.c simply with

python3 fact.py

If the test succeeds, the script's return code will be 0.

Congratulations! You have now tested some C code with Python! 🎉

Enter pytest¶

We are not here to just play around with bare asserts. I promised you the full power of Python and pytest, so we can't settle with just this simple example. Let's add pytest to our test dependencies and do this instead

# file: test_fact.py

from ctypes import CDLL

import pytest

@pytest.fixture
def libfact():
    yield CDLL("./fact.so")


def test_fact(libfact):
    assert libfact.fact(6) == 720
    assert libfact.fact(0) == 1
    assert libfact.fact(-42) == 1

Now run pytest to get

$ pytest
=========================== test session starts ============================
platform linux -- Python 3.10.2, pytest-7.0.0, pluggy-1.0.0
rootdir: /tmp
collected 1 item

test_fact.py .                                                       [100%]

============================ 1 passed in 0.00s =============================

That's some more informative output than what a plain Python test script would give us! How about starting to leverage some of the other pytest features, like parametrised tests? Let's rewrite our test case like so

# file: test_fact.py

from ctypes import CDLL

import pytest


@pytest.fixture
def libfact():
    yield CDLL("./fact.so")


@pytest.mark.parametrize("n,e", [(6, 720), (0, 1), (-42, 1)])
def test_fact(libfact, n, e):
    assert libfact.fact(n) == e

Let's run this again with pytest, this time with a more verbose output:

pytest -vv
=========================== test session starts ============================
platform linux -- Python 3.10.2, pytest-7.0.0, pluggy-1.0.0 -- /tmp/.venv/bin/python3.10
cachedir: .pytest_cache
rootdir: /tmp
collected 3 items

test_fact.py::test_fact[6-720] PASSED                                [ 33%]
test_fact.py::test_fact[0-1] PASSED                                  [ 66%]
test_fact.py::test_fact[-42-1] PASSED                                [100%]

============================ 3 passed in 0.01s =============================

Sweet! 🍯

In the wild¶

Thus far we've got an idea of how to invoke C from Python and how to write some simple tests that we can run with pytest while also leveraging features like fixtures and parametrised tests. Let us now step this up a notch and consider the organisation of sources within an actual C project, for instance

my-c-project/
├── docs/
├── src/    <- All *.c and *.h sources, perhaps organised into sub-folders
├── tests/  <- Our test sources, obviously!
├── ChangeLog
├── configure.ac
├── LICENCE
├── Makefile.am
├── README
...

In the previous example, we built the shared object fact.so by hand, but in a CI environment we would probably want to automate that step too. What should we use for that? A bash script? A makefile? Python, of course! What else?!? 😀

Let's make our sample C sources slightly more interesting. For example, we could borrow a few parts of the cache.c and cache.h sources from Austin, which implement a simple LRU cache. This is part of the spec

// file: src/cache.h

#ifndef CACHE_H
#define CACHE_H

#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

typedef uintptr_t key_dt;
typedef void *value_t;

typedef struct queue_item_t
{
    struct queue_item_t *prev, *next;
    key_dt key;
    value_t value; // Takes ownership of a free-able object
} queue_item_t;

typedef struct queue_t
{
    unsigned count;
    unsigned capacity;
    queue_item_t *front, *rear;
    void (*deallocator)(value_t);
} queue_t;

queue_item_t *
queue_item_new(value_t, key_dt);

void
queue_item__destroy(queue_item_t *, void (*)(value_t));

queue_t *
queue_new(int, void (*)(value_t));

int
queue__is_full(queue_t *);

int
queue__is_empty(queue_t *);

value_t
queue__dequeue(queue_t *);

queue_item_t *
queue__enqueue(queue_t *, value_t, key_dt);

void
queue__destroy(queue_t *);

and this is the corresponding part of the implementation

// file: src/cache.c

#include <stdbool.h>
#include <stdio.h>

#include "cache.h"

#define isvalid(x) ((x) != NULL)

// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
queue_item_t *
queue_item_new(value_t value, key_dt key)
{
    queue_item_t *item = (queue_item_t *)calloc(1, sizeof(queue_item_t));

    item->value = value;
    item->key = key;

    return item;
}

// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
void
queue_item__destroy(queue_item_t *self, void (*deallocator)(value_t))
{
    if (!isvalid(self))
        return;

    deallocator(self->value);

    free(self);
}

// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
queue_t *
queue_new(int capacity, void (*deallocator)(value_t))
{
    queue_t *queue = (queue_t *)calloc(1, sizeof(queue_t));

    queue->capacity = capacity;
    queue->deallocator = deallocator;

    return queue;
}

// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
int
queue__is_full(queue_t *queue)
{
    return queue->count == queue->capacity;
}

// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
int
queue__is_empty(queue_t *queue)
{
    return queue->rear == NULL;
}

// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
value_t
queue__dequeue(queue_t *queue)
{
    if (queue__is_empty(queue))
        return NULL;

    if (queue->front == queue->rear)
        queue->front = NULL;

    queue_item_t *temp = queue->rear;
    queue->rear = queue->rear->prev;

    if (queue->rear)
        queue->rear->next = NULL;

    void *value = temp->value;
    free(temp);

    queue->count--;

    return value;
}

// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
queue_item_t *
queue__enqueue(queue_t *self, value_t value, key_dt key)
{
    if (queue__is_full(self))
        return NULL;

    queue_item_t *temp = queue_item_new(value, key);
    temp->next = self->front;

    if (queue__is_empty(self))
        self->rear = self->front = temp;
    else
    {
        self->front->prev = temp;
        self->front = temp;
    }

    self->count++;

    return temp;
}

// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
void
queue__destroy(queue_t *self)
{
    if (!isvalid(self))
        return;

    queue_item_t *next = NULL;
    for (queue_item_t *item = self->front; isvalid(item); item = next)
    {
        next = item->next;
        queue_item__destroy(item, self->deallocator);
    }

    free(self);
}

It's quite a fair bit of code; however, we are not interested in how the data structures are implemented, but rather to what it actually implements. This already gives us plenty to play with.

The important detail here is that our C application has a component implemented in cache.c and we want to unit-test it. Before we can run any actual tests, we need to build a binary object that we can invoke from Python. So let's put this code in tests/cunit/__init__.py

from pathlib import Path
from subprocess import PIPE, STDOUT, run

HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
TEST = HERE.parent
ROOT = TEST.parent
SRC = ROOT / "src"


class CompilationError(Exception):
    pass


def compile(source: Path, cflags=[], ldadd=[]):
    binary = source.with_suffix(".so")

    result = run(
        ["gcc", "-shared", *cflags, "-o", str(binary), str(source), *ldadd],
        stdout=PIPE,
        stderr=STDOUT,
        cwd=SRC,
    )

    if result.returncode == 0:
        return

    raise CompilationError(result.stdout.decode())

This simply defines the compile utility that allows us to invoke gcc to compile a source and generate the .so shared object. We can then use it in our test source this way

from ctypes import CDLL

import pytest
from tests.cunit import SRC, compile

C = CDLL("libc.so.6")


@pytest.fixture
def cache():
    source = SRC / "cache.c"
    compile(source)
    yield CDLL(str(source.with_suffix(".so")))


def test_cache(cache):
    lru_cache = cache.lru_cache_new(10, C.free)
    assert lru_cache
    cache.lru_cache__destroy(lru_cache)

At this point, your project folder should have the following structure

my-c-project/
...
├── src/
|   ├── cache.c
|   └── cache.h
├── tests/
|   ├── cunit/
|   |   ├── __init__.py
|   |   └── test_cache.py
|   └── __init__.py
...

and when you run pytest again, this time the C source would be compiled at runtime using gcc. The tests then run as before, which should produce the same output we saw earlier.

Dead end?¶

If you're still with me, then things are probably looking interesting to you too. So let's test a bit more of the functions exported by the caching component. Let's make a test case for the queue_item_t and queue_t objects, like so

from ctypes import CDLL

import pytest
from tests.cunit import SRC, compile

C = CDLL("libc.so.6")


@pytest.fixture
def cache():
    source = SRC / "cache.c"
    compile(source)
    yield CDLL(str(source.with_suffix(".so")))


NULL = 0


def test_queue_item(cache):
    value = 1
    queue_item = cache.queue_item_new(value, 42)
    assert queue_item

    cache.queue_item__destroy(queue_item, C.free)


@pytest.mark.parametrize("qsize", [0, 10, 100, 1000])
def test_queue(cache, qsize):
    q = cache.queue_new(qsize, C.free)

    assert cache.queue__is_empty(q)
    assert qsize == 0 or not cache.queue__is_full(q)

    assert cache.queue__dequeue(q) is NULL

    values = [C.malloc(16) for _ in range(qsize)]
    assert all(values)

    for k, v in enumerate(values):
        assert cache.queue__enqueue(q, v, k)

    assert qsize == 0 or not cache.queue__is_empty(q)
    assert cache.queue__is_full(q)
    assert cache.queue__enqueue(q, 42, 42) is NULL

    assert values == [cache.queue__dequeue(q) for _ in range(qsize)]

If you want to figure out for yourself where the problem is, pause here. When you are ready to carry on, change line 20 to

and now the tests will all be happy! However, we really want to avoid crashing the pytest process when we run into a segmentation fault, which is not so rare when running arbitrary C code. Not only that, but we would like to get some useful information, like a traceback, that could give us insight as to where the problem might be! One of the many strengths of pytest is its extensive configuration API. How do we use it to not crash the test runner? The idea is to spawn another pytest process that runs just a test. Now, if that test causes a segmentation fault, the parent process will keep running the other tests. Let's put this into tests/cunit/conftest.py

# file: tests/cunit/conftest.py

import os
import sys
from subprocess import PIPE, run
from types import FunctionType


class SegmentationFault(Exception):
    pass


class CUnitTestFailure(Exception):
    pass


def pytest_pycollect_makeitem(collector, name, obj):
    if (
        not os.getenv("PYTEST_CUNIT")
        and isinstance(obj, FunctionType)
        and name.startswith("test_")
    ):
        obj.__cunit__ = (str(collector.fspath), name)


def cunit(module: str, name: str, full_name: str):
    def _(*_, **__):
        test = f"{module}::{name}"
        env = os.environ.copy()
        env["PYTEST_CUNIT"] = full_name

        result = run([sys.argv[0], "-svv", test], stdout=PIPE, stderr=PIPE, env=env)

        if result.returncode == 0:
            return

        raise CUnitTestFailure("\n" + result.stdout.decode())

    return _


def pytest_collection_modifyitems(session, config, items) -> None:
    if test_name := os.getenv("PYTEST_CUNIT"):
        # We are inside the sandbox process. We select the only test we care
        items[:] = [_ for _ in items if _.name == test_name]
        return

    for item in items:
        if hasattr(item._obj, "__cunit__"):
            item._obj = cunit(*item._obj.__cunit__, full_name=item.name)

But what is the conftest.py code actually doing? Let's have a look. The pytest_pycollect_makeitem hook gets invoked when the tests inside tests\cunit are being collected by pytest. At this stage we "mark" them as C unit tests by giving each collected item the __cunit__ attribute. The value is a tuple containing the information of where the item came from (collection.fspath is the path of the module that defined the test, e.g. tests/cunit/test_cache.py) and the test name (e.g. test_queue_item). In our case we only care about items that are of FunctionType type and that start with test_. The environment variable PYTEST_CUNIT is used to detect whether we are running in the parent pytest process or the "sandbox" child. In the latter case we don't care of marking tests because we know exactly what we want to run.

Once all the tests have been collected, we use the pytest_collection_modifyitems hook to actually modify the tests that we previously marked as C unit tests. Again, the behaviour depends on whether we are in the parent pytest process, or in the sandbox. If PYTEST_CUNIT is set, that's the signal that we are in the child pytest process. The value, as we shall see shortly, contains the information needed to pick the test that we want to run. So we use it to modify the list items to just the test that matches the information stored in PYTEST_CUNIT. In the parent pytest process we actually modify what the items that we marked as C unit tests do. Obviously, we don't want them to run the actual test, but rather a new instance of pytest that will then run the test on behalf of the parent process. The magic happens inside the "decorator" cunit, which we use to build a closure around the test that we want to run. As you can see, it returns a function (with a bit of a funny and unusual signature) which, when called, will set the PYTEST_CUNIT variable with the full name of the test (this is to support parametrised tests) and then run sys.argv[0] (which should be pytest if we run the test suite with pytest), followed by the switches -svv and the path of the module that provides the test we are wrapping around. This way, when the process terminates, either because the test passed or something really bad happened, we can inspect the return code and the streams, and act accordingly.

So now we have a test runner that can handle segmentation faults gracefully but still doesn't tell us where they actually happened. Can we get some more detailed information in the output? When a Python test fails we get a nice traceback that tells us where things went wrong. Can we do the same with C unit tests? The answer is yes, provided we collect core dumps while tests run. If you are running on Ubuntu, you can do ulimit -c unlimited and a core dump will be generated in the working directory every time a segmentation fault occurs. We can then run gdb in batch mode to print a nice traceback that will hopefully help us investigate the problem. So let's add these helpers to the conftest.py file

from pathlib import Path
from subprocess import STDOUT, check_output


def gdb(cmds: list[str], *args: str) -> str:
    return check_output(
        ["gdb", "-q", "-batch"]
        + [_ for cs in (("-ex", _) for _ in cmds) for _ in cs]
        + list(args),
        stderr=STDOUT,
    ).decode()


def bt(binary: Path) -> str:
    if Path("core").is_file():
        return gdb(["bt full", "q"], str(binary), "core")
    return "No core dump available."

Pythonic C unit testing¶

OK, running C unit tests is nice and fun, but it doesn't save us much in terms of typing. In fact, the tests we wrote so far not only feel quite verbose, considering we are writing Python code, but don't feel Pythonic at all. Whilst there is, in principle, no reason why non-Python tests written in Python should look and feel Pythonic, can we somehow do something perhaps more elegant? The idea of using a fixture to wrap around a binary object is perhaps interesting, but can we maybe pretend that cache is a Python module instead so that we can do things like from cache import queue_item_new etc... and sweep all this ctypes business under the carpet? Well, let's give this a try, shall we?

Back in tests/cunit/__init__.py, let's add the following subtype of ModuleType:

from ctypes import CDLL
from types import ModuleType


class CModule(ModuleType):
    def __init__(self, source):
        super().__init__(source.name, f"Generated from {source.with_suffix('.c')}")
        self.__binary__ = CDLL(source.with_suffix(".so"))
        print(self.__binary__.__dict__)

    def __getattr__(self, name):
        return getattr(self.__binary__, name)

    @classmethod
    def compile(cls, source, cflags=[], ldadd=[]):
        compile(source.with_suffix(".c"), cflags, ldadd)
        return cls(source)
